strengths: Strong empirical results across diverse benchmarks (synthetic corruptions, real-world shifts, semantic shifts) with significant improvements in calibration metrics (e.g., 40% ACE reduction on Camelyon17)

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation including ablation studies, sensitivity analyses across hyperparameters, and evaluation on multiple architectures (ResNets, DenseNets, ViT, Swin, DeiT)
Well-motivated technical approach combining frequency-domain insights with principled gradient-based optimization; asymmetric treatment of ID calibration as first-order constraint is novel
Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation details, complete pseudocode, hyperparameter tables, and code release promise; extensive appendix (25 pages) with sensitivity analyses
Practical efficiency: two-stage fine-tuning requires only 0.29 hours; training-from-scratch adds ~18% overhead, making approach viable for real applications
Formal theoretical characterization via Proposition 4.1 providing exact optimizer-level statement of projection property
Effective presentation with compelling visualizations (Grad-CAM heatmaps, reliability diagrams) clearly illustrating the method's benefits
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: DCT-based filtering for robustness (Li et al. 2023, Wang et al. 2023) and gradient conflict resolution (PCGrad, CAGrad) are established ideas; contribution is primarily in combination rather than fundamental innovation

Weak theoretical guarantees: Proposition 4.1 only ensures first-order non-increase L_calib ≤ L_calib + O(η²), which could be violated for non-infinitesimal step sizes; no analysis of why frequency filtering fundamentally improves shift robustness; gap between theory (ignoring ε) and implementation (including ε for stability) is unaddressed

Limited effectiveness on semantic shift: Office-Home improvements are modest (ECE 20.41 vs. 21.09-22.92 for baselines), suggesting method is primarily for low-level corruptions; no analysis of which shift types benefit most

Unjustified hyperparameter design choices: start epoch selection (200) lacks principled guidance; filtering ratio ρ=0.05 appears arbitrary despite being the dominant trade-off parameter; Soft-ECE temperature t=0.1 fixed without sensitivity study; DCT λ∈{15,18,25} random sampling lacks justification
Misleading 'hard constraint' terminology: ID calibration is actually a soft first-order constraint that could be violated for large step sizes; overstated in abstract/introduction

Incomplete multi-objective comparison: PCGrad sometimes outperforms FGR on accuracy (88.68% vs. 87.37% on Camelyon17); inadequate explanation of when/why asymmetric approach is preferable to careful symmetric weighting
Limited scope: image classification only; DCT-specific to images; requires training data access (cannot directly calibrate existing pre-trained models); doesn't handle unknown-class OOD detection
Statistical rigor concerns: only 3 random seeds with no confidence intervals or significance tests; some improvements modest (e.g., iWildCam 3.34 vs. 3.50) without validation

Batch-size dependency and interpretability gaps: gradient rectification depends on batch composition (smaller batches perform better but need accumulation); Grad-CAM visualization limited to few examples; connection between frequency filtering and semantic feature learning lacks rigorous validation

Heuristic conflict detection: using dot product g_main·g_calib < 0 lacks justification versus alternative divergence measures; gradient conflict rate analysis (Figure 6) suggests potential instability during training

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (CIFAR, Tiny-ImageNet, WILDS, Office-Home), architectures (CNNs and transformers), and calibration metrics (ECE, CECE, ACE)
Extensive ablation studies and sensitivity analyses demonstrating necessity of both components and behavior under hyperparameter variations
Well-motivated problem addressing practical challenge of maintaining calibration under distribution shifts without target domain access
Theoretical grounding via Proposition 4.1 with formal proof showing first-order ID calibration preservation
Practical contributions including two-stage fine-tuning strategy and computational complexity analysis (18% overhead)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and thorough appendices providing implementation details
weaknesses: Limited novelty: DCT-based filtering and gradient-based multi-objective optimization are well-established; asymmetric constraint alone insufficient for major conference contribution

Weak theoretical guarantees: Proposition 4.1 only guarantees O(η²) preservation for 'sufficiently small' step sizes—never quantified and never empirically validated; inapplicable to adaptive optimizers

Inconsistent empirical improvements: Substantial gains on synthetic corruptions (20-40% ECE reduction) but modest on realistic WILDS datasets (4-10% improvement) and semantic shifts, contradicting broad applicability claims
Misleading 'target-agnostic' claim: Requires tuning multiple dataset-specific hyperparameters (ρ, γ, E_start) without guidance on selection without target domain knowledge

Experimental design flaws: (1) No statistical significance testing despite 3-run averaging; (2) No error bars; (3) Different methods optimized for different shift types; (4) Starting FGR at epoch 200 implicitly uses knowledge of training distribution

Methodological concerns: Gradient computation inconsistency between D_mix and D_orig (Eq. 8) not addressed; batch statistics compatibility unclear; choice of Soft-ECE arbitrary (Table 16 shows similar performance with other losses)

Limited theoretical insight: No explanation of why frequency filtering + gradient rectification specifically works; Figure 6 shows correlation not causation; Grad-CAM visualizations cherry-picked without quantitative analysis
Scope limitations undermine impact: (1) Image classification only; (2) Poor performance on semantic shifts; (3) No unknown-class OOD detection; (4) Hyperparameter selection procedure not specified
Reproducibility concerns: No code link provided despite claims; many dataset-specific hyperparameters (Tables 9-10); λ randomly sampled adding variability not reflected in statistics

Insufficient comparison with recent baselines: MaxEnt Loss (Neo et al., 2024) achieves competitive results; Table 4 shows symmetric methods (PCGrad) sometimes achieve higher accuracy, questioning asymmetric constraint value

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear intuition: distribution shifts exploit high-frequency shortcuts; suppressing them improves calibration
Theoretically grounded gradient rectification mechanism (Proposition 4.1) with formal first-order guarantee; elegant asymmetric design outperforms symmetric alternatives
Exceptionally comprehensive experimental validation: 8+ datasets across synthetic/real/semantic shifts, multiple architectures (CNNs and transformers), extensive ablations and sensitivity analyses
Strong and consistent empirical results: 40% ACE reduction on Camelyon17, 2.36% ECE on iWildCam, maintains ID calibration while improving OOD performance
Practical efficiency with two-stage fine-tuning (0.29h overhead); enables deployment on pretrained models
High-quality presentation with clear motivation, effective visualizations (Grad-CAM), comprehensive appendix, and honest discussion of limitations
Thorough analysis revealing mechanism (gradient conflict dynamics, Wasserstein distance analysis, comparison with symmetric methods)
weaknesses: Limited novelty in core components: DCT filtering from Li et al. (2023), gradient projection from PCGrad/CAGrad; main contribution is asymmetric combination (incremental for ICML)
Weak semantic shift performance (Office-Home ECE 6.32% vs 6.56% BSCE-GRA); many real-world shifts are semantic not textural, limiting practical applicability
Hyperparameter complexity despite 'weight-free' claims: dataset-dependent γ (Tables 9-10), ρ (0.05 vs 0.1), start epoch (200/350), plus randomized λ; no principled selection guidance

Insufficient theoretical justification for design choices: no empirical comparison of filtering approaches (DCT vs alternatives), why M=15 bins, why ρ varies by dataset, when first-order approximation (Eq. 12) holds

Incomplete validation of core assumption: no frequency domain analysis showing filtered images remove spurious patterns; only Grad-CAM visualization; Wasserstein analysis shows ρ dominates but doesn't validate filtering hypothesis
18.5% computational overhead for from-scratch training (1.92h vs 1.62h baseline) comparable to or exceeding some baselines; DCT + dual gradient computation non-negligible
Restricted scope: image classification only; DCT-based approach doesn't generalize to other modalities; semantic shift gains are modest
Start epoch selection (200/350) appears arbitrary; warm-up wastes 57% of training; limited guidance for new training schedules; two-stage approach mitigates but requires pretrained models
